text: At 10,000 phones, the database sat at 93% CPU.
say: At ten thousand phones, the database sat at ninety-three percent C P U.

text: Each request cost it 22 milliseconds of work.
say: Each request cost it twenty-two milliseconds of work.

text: The easy fix was a bigger machine, and I fixed the code instead.
And the answers had to stay exactly the same.
I ranked the database's busiest statements by their share of total time, not by their average speed.
Search, Discover and feed shares came out on top, with more than half of it.
They now read a page's keys first, then fetch only those rows.
A search of one or two letters skips the fuzzy-match index entirely.
Likes, saves, shares, comments and follows each run four fewer statements.
Before merging, 392 recorded responses from the old code had to match the new code exactly.
say: Before merging, three hundred ninety-two recorded responses from the old code had to match the new code exactly.

text: Then the same test ran again, on the same machine.

say: Database C P U fell from ninety-three percent to forty-four.

text: Work per request fell from 22 milliseconds to 10.
say: Work per request fell from twenty-two milliseconds to ten.

text: For a free member, a search on a single letter went from 3,310 milliseconds of database time to 54.
say: For a free member, a search on a single letter went from three thousand three hundred and ten milliseconds of database time to fifty-four.
